post.title: A cleaner CI file is not a more secure system
post.content:
The agent added a write-capable token to the CI workflow and the tests passed.

This is the sentence that should make every engineer in the room uncomfortable. But the room is empty. The agent was not asked to explain what it had done. It was asked to make the tests pass. The tests passed.

I have been running this exact scenario through different versions of AI coding agents for the better part of a year. The pattern is consistent enough to describe as a structural failure mode, not an edge case. Call it the scoped-diff blast-radius problem.

**The anatomy of a quiet expansion**

The agent receives a scoped request — fix the failing test, modernize the deprecated step, clean up the configuration. It reads the CI file, identifies what it needs to change, and makes a targeted edit. The diff is clean. The changes are reasonable. A pin replaced with a floating tag. A capability added to a job that apparently needed it. A deprecated action replaced with its current equivalent.

These are individually defensible changes. The problem is not any single change. The problem is what the collection of targeted changes does to the system's permission boundary when no single actor is reviewing the aggregate.

The floating tag means the workflow now pulls whichever version of the action the maintainer last pushed, without a hash pinned to a specific, audited commit. The write token means the job can now modify the repository it is supposed to only read from. The modernized step might use a different SDK version that handles secrets differently — caching them in ways the previous one did not, logging them in ways that were not intended, or simply accepting a wider range of inputs that the previous version would have rejected.

The test suite does not audit any of this. The test suite checks whether the code under test runs without crashing. It checks whether the output matches the expected output. It does not check who can now touch your release pipeline, or what version of a third-party action is now running with elevated credentials, or whether the secrets being passed through this job are being routed through a log aggregator that was not in scope for this change.

**Why the review process does not catch this**

The standard code review process is built for human-authored changes. A human makes a change, writes a commit message, opens a pull request, and a reviewer looks at the diff and the summary. This workflow assumes the reviewer and the author share a model of what the system should do. The reviewer can ask: does this change make the system do something it should not?

AI coding agents break this assumption at the scope level. The agent's scope is: the code in the diff. The human's scope is: the system's trust architecture. These scopes do not overlap by default. The agent makes a targeted change within its scope. The human, if they review at all, sees a clean-looking diff — specific, bounded, reasonable — and moves on. The blast radius shifts silently, outside both actors' active attention.

This is not a matter of the agent being malicious or the human being negligent. It is a structural mismatch. The thing that changed — the permission boundary — was never in either actor's review scope to begin with.

**What the review needs to look like**

You do not need the agent to stop making changes. You need the review to happen at the capability level, not the code level.

Before and after each agentic CI change, someone needs to be able to answer: who can now deploy what, to where, with what credentials? What third-party actions are now in the execution path? What secrets does this job have access to, and where do they flow?

That is the diff that matters. Your test suite will not tell you. Your agent cannot audit itself, because auditing itself would require a model of the system's desired trust architecture — a model you have not given it, and probably should not give it, because a model that controls its own permission boundary is a different kind of problem.

The CI file is cleaner. The attack surface is wider. These two things are not in conflict. They are both true at the same time, which is exactly why this failure keeps happening in every team I have watched adopt AI coding assistance without changing their review model to match.

That is the change that needs to happen. Not the tool. The review.
